    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools. You’ll work closely with the engineers who build those tools, and with our Platform and SRE teams.

    AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents. The team’s first priority is making it reliable, observable, and fair between tenants at agent scale, and helping redesign it for that scale without breaking the tools that depend on it. Depending on your experience, you’ll own major parts of that work or lead it. Alongside it, the team builds the backend services that give every branch of a project the configuration and secrets it needs.

    Industry observers note that we want to be upfront: this role carries real operational load. Our on-call process and rotation are newly introduced and need a lot of maturing, and you’ll help build them into something sustainable from your first weeks. You’ll be on call for services on the critical path, and incidents come before planned work. Platform teams run the infrastructure underneath; you’ll own the services themselves, from their code to how they behave in production. It’s ideal for someone who enjoys that kind of ownership, thrives in async, fast-paced environments, and stays calm when the root cause turns out to be in someone else’s system.

    Industry observers note that help mature the team’s on-call from your first weeks: grow the rotation to cover every service the team runs, write runbooks, and agree when to declare an incident. Then build it, with our embedded SRE, into a sustainable follow-the-sun rotation as the team grows.

    Set SLOs with the teams that call the service, and build the observability to hold them: metrics per tenant and per caller, alerts that catch failures wherever they start, and logs you can search across regions.

    Make deploys routine with canary and staged rollouts, so dependency and security upgrades stop being risky.

    Redesign how the service works with Postgres at scale: reusing connections, limiting or streaming large results, and isolating and rate-limiting tenants, so no single caller, human or agent, can degrade it for everyone else.

    Help decide the service’s long-term architecture with our Platform teams, then evolve it without breaking the callers that depend on it.

    Write down and agree the service’s contract with its callers, including the dashboard, MCP and AI, and platform workers: how transactions, multi-statement queries, timeouts, and errors behave.

    Work through incidents with the networking, Kubernetes, pooler, and control-plane teams when a problem on the path to customers’ databases starts in their systems.

    Build backend services for code-first workflows, starting with delivering each branch’s configuration and secrets to the services that need them.

    Make small changes directly in the CLI, dashboard, or docs when a capability needs them, with the owning team reviewing.

    Review code and designs, mentor other engineers, and grow into leading the team’s technical direction.

    Have 5+ years of experience as a software engineer, most of it building and running backend services in production.

    Have run a high-traffic, multi-tenant service in production: been on call for it, worked incidents through to resolution, and followed through on postmortems.

    Write strong TypeScript, and work confidently in a large Node.js backend codebase.

    Understand Postgres from the client side: connection management and pooling, transactions, statement timeouts and cancellation, and large result sets.

    Have built observability for a service you owned (metrics, tracing, logs, and alerts tied to SLOs), and used it to debug problems that span proxies, load balancers, or Kubernetes.

    Have kept a service healthy under load with patterns such as rate limiting, timeouts, memory limits, and graceful degradation.

    Have shipped changes to a live service safely, with canaries, staged rollouts, feature flags, or fast rollback.

    Work calmly and constructively with other teams during incidents, including when the root cause is in a system you don’t own.

    Communicate clearly in writing, from design docs to postmortems, thrive in async, globally distributed teams, and make progress when the path isn’t fully defined.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have rebuilt or migrated a live, high-traffic service without breaking its callers, using techniques such as shadow traffic, contract tests, or incremental replacement.

    Have led the design of reliability work, such as tenant isolation, load shedding, or a staged-deploy pipeline, or set technical direction that other engineers built on.

    Have built or operated a database proxy or connection pooler (such as PgBouncer, Supavisor, or pgcat), or an API gateway such as Envoy.

    Have secured a service that runs SQL on its callers’ behalf: handling credentials safely, and limiting how much damage any one caller can do.

    Production experience in a second backend language, such as Elixir or Go.

    Experience with a secrets manager or key management service, such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS KMS.

    Familiarity with Supabase, or with how AI agents use databases through tools like MCP.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    In a recent development, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Survey: Organizations Report Positive ROI on AI Investments, Yet Data Readiness and Oversight Lag Behind

    📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.
    • According to recent reports, the company's recent State of Enterprise AI Maturity research surveyed 515 U.S.-based AI decision-makers.
    • According to recent reports, the findings suggest that gaining value from individual AI applications and preparing to operate them more broadly are separate challenges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.

    According to recent reports, the company's recent State of Enterprise AI Maturity research surveyed 515 U.S.-based AI decision-makers. Just 5% believed their organizations' data was largely ready for AI.

    According to recent reports, the findings suggest that gaining value from individual AI applications and preparing to operate them more broadly are separate challenges. Reported returns alone do not establish that an organization has the foundations to sustain or expand those results.

    Recent findings suggest that further found that 37% of respondents' organizations had paused, scaled back, or abandoned an underperforming AI initiative in the previous 12 months. Among that group, data quality or availability was the most frequently cited main reason, at 24%.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, 29% reported completing a formal data audit and remediation plan. The research also placed 69% of organizations in the exploring, experimenting, or implementing stages of adoption.

    Further distinguishes data prepared for conventional reporting from data prepared for AI. Its explanation emphasizes data origins and documentation, along with access controls that support ongoing evaluation and governance.

    For readers assessing their own readiness, the practical issue is whether data supports the requirements of a particular application. A collection suitable for a dashboard may need additional preparation before it can reliably support an AI system.

    It has been revealed that seventy-seven percent reported a positive return on AI investment. However, only 3% said their organizations had a documented AI-audit process.

    It has been revealed that the findings measure different things: perceived financial benefit and the existence of a repeatable oversight process. Neither substitutes for the other.

    Recent findings suggest that "In reality, confidence without a documented process is exposure," mentioned Kierra Dotson, associate director of AI strategy and governance at Further. "Closing that gap doesn't take upcoming technology; it requires an auditable governance process.".

    For the full report, visit the Further site (registration required).

    #89294. Breaking: Researchers Find AI Is Accelerating Vulnerability Discovery

    📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (488 w)

    AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Researchers Find AI Is Accelerating Vulnerability Discovery

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI-powered vulnerability research is contributing to a major increase in security updates, raising concerns that IT teams could fall behind as patching demands grow, according to cybersecurity organization ThreatDown.
    • In a recent blog post, the organization stated that in September 2026, vendors addressed 998 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) around Patch Tuesday, compared with 96 during the same period last year.
    • The researchers point to advanced AI models, including Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview, as a major factor behind the increase in vulnerability discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI-powered vulnerability research is contributing to a major increase in security updates, raising concerns that IT teams could fall behind as patching demands grow, according to cybersecurity organization ThreatDown.

    In a recent blog post, the organization stated that in September 2026, vendors addressed 998 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) around Patch Tuesday, compared with 96 during the same period last year. In addition, the three-month rolling average of patched Linux kernel vulnerabilities tripled year over year, while Google's Chrome browser experienced a 36-fold increase.

    The researchers point to advanced AI models, including Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview, as a major factor behind the increase in vulnerability discovery.

    Introduced in April 2026, Mythos Preview is being used through Project Glasswing, an initiative involving Microsoft, the Linux Foundation and other organizations to identify vulnerabilities in critical software.

    While AI could ultimately make software more secure, the cybersecurity organization warns that vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than organizations can deploy fixes.

    IT teams must still evaluate patches, test compatibility and schedule updates without disrupting critical business operations.

    The challenge is particularly significant for organizations already struggling with patch management.

    The cybersecurity vendor cites Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, which found that 35% of known actively exploited vulnerabilities remained unpatched after 28 days in 2025.

    Ryan Powell, vice president of IT and security at ThreatDown, remarked automated patching systems can help organizations manage the growing workload. However, additional patches still require more testing and validation, increasing operational overhead and the risks associated with frequent system changes.

    The report also highlights the risks of vulnerabilities in widely used software components such as OpenSSL, embedded in applications, network devices, and security products.

    Unlike standalone applications, these components often depend on downstream vendors to release updates before organizations can deploy fixes.

    According to recent reports, the security firm's analysis points to CVE-2022-0778, an OpenSSL vulnerability patched in March 2022, as an example. Some affected products did not receive updates until several months later.

    As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, these dependencies could delay remediation and extend organizations' exposure to known security flaws.

    ThreatDown's findings illustrate a growing challenge for enterprise cybersecurity: AI is making vulnerabilities easier to discover but fixing them remains a complex and time-consuming process.

    For the full report, visit the ThreatDown blog here.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

    Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

    Ransomware Attacks Move Beyond Enterprise Systems to Theaten Employees' Families

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (445 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a upcoming Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.
    • In a recent announcement, the company highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness.
    • The sample has an important limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a upcoming Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.

    In a recent announcement, the company highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness. Censuswide surveyed 1,200 information technology and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors in the first half of 2026.

    The sample has an important limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption. The results describe those victims' experiences, rather than the likelihood that an organization will suffer an attack. The report claims that sampling approach changed from previous studies.

    Semperis sells identity security, recovery and crisis management products.

    It has been revealed that the report claims 84% of respondents experienced attacks that exploited AI in some way. Its breakdown distinguishes AI-based attacks, reported by 40%, from attacks that manipulated victims' own AI agents or systems, reported by 44%. That distinction matters: The broader figure covers both attackers using AI and attackers exploiting AI deployed inside an organization.

    Recent findings suggest that defensive use of AI also produced mixed responses. Nearly half of respondents, 49%, said they successfully used AI for detection or response, while 23% said their AI tools failed to detect or respond successfully. Those are survey responses about victimized organizations, rather than a controlled comparison of security products.

    Chris Inglis, former U.S. national cyber director and a Semperis strategic adviser, described the difficulty of recognizing AI's involvement. "Many attacks are not perceived as being aided and abetted by AI because they're just too slick, too sophisticated," he stated in the report.

    Recent findings suggest that data erasure, destruction, or release remained the most frequently reported threat, at 56%. Blackmail, extortion or public shaming followed at 41%, with system lockouts or operational sabotage at 40%. The report also recorded psychological intimidation at 23% and physical threats at 17%.

    California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a newly introduced model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

    OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the company says has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

    Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity company NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.
    • The research firm's 2026 Worldwide AI Economics and Cost of Ownership Survey found that 69% reported such a gap, while only 15% had achieved an AI return on investment exceeding 100%.
    • In a separate May 2026 survey, 73% of respondents identified excessive AI costs as a significant risk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.

    The research firm's 2026 Worldwide AI Economics and Cost of Ownership Survey found that 69% reported such a gap, while only 15% had achieved an AI return on investment exceeding 100%.

    In a separate May 2026 survey, 73% of respondents identified excessive AI costs as a significant risk.

    IDC highlighted the findings in an October 20 analysis examining what enterprise customers expect from AI technology vendors.

    Enterprise customers are placing greater emphasis on measurable business outcomes when evaluating AI products, according to IDC.

    The firm identified three priorities for vendors: demonstrating financial value, addressing governance and security requirements, and building support beyond IT departments.

    In a recent development, the analysis also highlighted the gap between initial agentic AI deployments and broader adoption. Although 80% of organizations have started deploying agentic AI, only 17% are using it across the enterprise.

    IDC said evaluating AI investments can be difficult when the technology changes how employees work and how business processes operate.

    The firm expects AI infrastructure capacity to catch up with demand around 2029, potentially easing costs. Until then, vendors face pressure to demonstrate the long-term financial value of their products.

    In a recent development, AI funding decisions involve a broad range of executives. IDC's September 2026 C-Suite Tech Survey found that CIOs and CTOs were involved in 63% of those decisions, business-function executives in 62%, and chief financial officers in 61%.

    A separate IDC survey found that 42% of CEOs planned to hire a chief AI officer within the next 12 months.

    Sources indicate that buyers also reported concerns about the products and terms vendors offer. Limited integration with existing systems, insufficient model and data transparency, and concerns about vendor lock-in were each cited by 34% of respondents.

    Overpromising and underdelivering, along with unclear pricing models, were each cited by 31%.

    IDC mentioned vendors need to substantiate financial returns and address security and governance requirements while working with decision-makers across IT, finance, and other business departments.

    For more information, go to the IDC blog.

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

    Sources indicate that in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines latest guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security manufacturer SailPoint.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (615 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Report: Global Ransomware Attacks Rise 23% in Q3

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.
    • The organization's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.
    • Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    The organization's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.

    Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821. North America recorded the most attacks that month with 390, followed by Europe with 211.

    Sources indicate that the industrial sector accounted for 29% of quarterly attacks, while Qilin remained the most active ransomware group for the sixth consecutive quarter, recording 365 victims. The Gentlemen followed with 356, and INC Ransom ranked third with 109.

    The report highlighted a July cyber attack against a small UK power generation facility that forced operations to stop for approximately four days.

    Although the incident did not affect the national electricity grid, it demonstrated how cyber attacks can disrupt physical infrastructure.

    The security researchers remarked the incident was consistent with techniques previously associated with Iranian-affiliated campaigns, including attacks against internet-exposed industrial controllers.

    However, the UK government has not formally attributed the attack, and the techniques used remain unconfirmed.

    The report also identified growing security challenges as organizations connect traditional IT networks with operational technology (OT) systems for remote maintenance and centralized management.

    The firm recommended network segmentation, stronger privileged-access controls, and continuous monitoring of OT environments.

    The research found that more than 40 vulnerabilities affecting enterprise applications, VPN appliances, e-mail gateways, and management platforms were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog during the quarter.

    The report examined Gunra, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that has targeted 53 victims across multiple industries as of Q3.

    According to the cybersecurity tech giant, Gunra exploited vulnerabilities CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing Fortinet devices to gain access to corporate networks.

    The group also used stolen credentials, session hijacking, and administrative tools to move between systems before deploying ransomware.

    Other emerging ransomware groups included Deadlock and Storm, with the latter claiming 78 victims by the end of September.

    Researchers also observed initial access brokers advertising compromised VPN, Remote Desktop Protocol, and SSH access, alongside access to cloud identities, source code repositories, and security management platforms.

    The quarterly review also highlighted BraZetsu, an AI-enhanced Windows malware framework that evolved into a specialized initial access toolkit.

    According to the report, BraZetsu uses AI models to automate victim profiling, analyze compromised environments, and identify valuable corporate systems.

    The framework searches for enterprise software, financial data, digital certificates, and cloud credentials, helping operators identify compromised access that can be sold to other cyber criminals.

    The cybersecurity firm also identified risks involving legitimate AI agents, including prompt injection, excessive permissions, and unintended access to external systems.

    The report cited incidents involving U.S. and Australian government systems as examples of agents accessing resources beyond their intended scope.

    Researchers warned that these incidents do not necessarily involve malicious intent but can create consequences resembling conventional cyber intrusions.

    For the full report, visit the NCC Group site.

    California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a new model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

    OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the company notes has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

    Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity company NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

    Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft is introducing fresh tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.
    • In a recent development, in a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments.
    • "Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft is introducing fresh tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

    In a recent development, in a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

    "Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

    According to recent reports, one of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

    Sources indicate that microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

    The company is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. Newly introduced capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

    The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

    As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

    That initiative introduces aims for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

    "Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," remarked Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

    It has been revealed that project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

    In a recent development, taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The company is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

    Phillips stated AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

    Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

    According to recent reports, in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines latest guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security firm SailPoint.

    #89252. Cisco Intros Privileged Infrastructure Access for People and AI Agents

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (606 w)

    Cisco Intros Privileged Infrastructure Access for People and AI Agents

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.
    • In a recent blog post, Cisco's Matt Caulfield described a system that uses cryptographic identity to connect an administrator or agent to the infrastructure needed for a particular task.
    • In a recent development, "If there is no work being done, no privilege exists," Caulfield wrote.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    In a recent blog post, Cisco's Matt Caulfield described a system that uses cryptographic identity to connect an administrator or agent to the infrastructure needed for a particular task. Access is governed by short-lived privileges, with session recording providing a record of the work performed.

    In a recent development, "If there is no work being done, no privilege exists," Caulfield wrote. Cisco positions the offering as a way to bring identity controls directly into infrastructure operations while reducing dependence on static credentials, shared secrets, and broad access.

    The announcement follows Cisco's previously unveiled Teleport partnership and its Infrastructure Identity concept, which connects the identity of a person or machine with the resources it can access, the actions it performs, and the permissions governing those actions.

    Sources indicate that caulfield described a gap between the controls organizations apply to workforce applications and those used to administer network infrastructure. Companies have invested in single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and risk-based controls for application access, he wrote, but those protections often do not follow an engineer logging into a router or switch.

    Instead, infrastructure access may depend on long-lived credentials, shared accounts, or separate policy systems. According to Cisco, that separation makes it harder to enforce least privilege and establish which person or system performed a particular action.

    The firm illustrates the problem with an administrator updating hundreds of switches during a maintenance window. If some updates fail, the administrator needs to troubleshoot before the window closes. The permissions available to handle that work, however, may cover more infrastructure and remain active longer than the task requires.

    According to recent reports, traditional privileged access management can reduce risk through credential vaulting and rotation, Caulfield wrote. But he argued that operational friction can undermine those controls when teams create exceptions to complete urgent work. Those exceptions can leave credentials and privileges usable after the immediate need has passed.

    In a recent development, cisco's stated objective is to give infrastructure teams a consistent route to the devices they manage while providing security teams with policy enforcement, temporary permissions, and a record of activity. The organization describes operational convenience as part of the design, rather than treating access governance solely as a credential-management problem.

    Industry observers note that privileged Infrastructure Access makes access an on-demand action, according to the announcement. Cryptographic identity establishes the actor, and the resulting connection provides only the privileges needed to complete the task. Those privileges expire when the task concludes.

    In a recent development, for customers using Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) and Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+), the offering can draw on existing policy and device context to govern access to Cisco routers and switches. Cisco notes customers can extend the same access model to other infrastructure, including servers, Kubernetes clusters, and cloud resources.

    California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a latest model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

    OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the organization says has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

    Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity tech giant NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

    7 Holiday Decor Trends Designers Say We're About to See Everywhere

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pictured above: A holiday-ready space by designer Marie Flanigan.
    • Christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh.
    • However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pictured above: A holiday-ready space by designer Marie Flanigan.

    Christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh. This year, on-trend doesn’t have to mean brand-new—designers love decorating with heirloom pieces collected over time.

    However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.

    This winter, our decor is taking a note from European culture—again. Swedish folk art is emerging as a hot winter trend in both holiday and home decor. Defined by bold red hues, tulip motifs, and S-scrolls, the style blends cozy-core with the heritage style craze.

    Recent findings suggest that “European folk influences are so massive right now,” states designer Johanna Lyle of Jo Lyle & Co. “Think Swedish Dala horses, quilt motifs, and decorative stitching. I think we will see those continue into holiday decor.”.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to her tree decor, interior designer Francesca Grace waves a hand at the carefully contrived, and she’s not alone. “My ornaments are collected from my travels, so the tree is really a collection of memories. I love unpacking them and remembering where each one came from. They don’t all match, and I wouldn’t want them to,” indicates Grace. “I let the ornaments lead. That mix feels much more personal to me, and it gives the tree something new to say as the collection grows.” This year’s trends hinge on antiqued, inherited style, with one-off pieces that channel bold character and hardly ever come with a matching set.

    Interior designer Marie Flanigan likes to add a fresh twist to her seasonal decor with dried oranges and pops of cranberry red.

    “We've seen such a beautiful resurgence of dried citrus in holiday decorating over the past few years,” Flanigan explains. “And I think cranberries are ready for their moment to shine. Their rich red hue feels especially festive, and I love the idea of incorporating them into fresh greenery, draping them across a mantel, or pairing them with dried oranges for a more layered look.”.

    According to recent reports, if there’s one classic Christmas element Grace hopes makes a comeback, it's multicolored lights. Inherently nostalgic, these bold-hued bulbs were a ’90s staple.

    “I’m ready for a little less restraint on the tree. Those reds, blues, greens, and yellows immediately bring back the feeling of Christmas as a child. They also pull together a collection of ornaments that might otherwise seem completely unrelated. White lights can be beautiful, but I want my Christmas tree to have some mischief,” states Grace.

    The classic red-and-green combination may take the title for the most iconic holiday palette, but this year, color trends are going complementary. While base colors stay warm and slightly rusted, patterned pieces are taking on cooler tones. This year, we’re also trading traditional plaid for Scottish tartan.

    “Warm crimsons, rich browns, tactile fabrics, and blue-green plaids make a beautiful holiday palette,” says Elizabeth Bennett, cofounder of the interior design firm Kobel + Co.

    In a total rejection of mass-manufactured everything, handmade felt pieces are taking holiday homes by storm. The style has even coined a upcoming holiday aesthetic: #Kitschmas, and, according to Lyle, it’s here to stay. “As AI continues to homogenize design, things made by humans will feel more special and important. Handmade and crafted items create stories around decor that feel meaningful and can be treasured year after year,” she indicates.

    Industry observers note that moody browns are steadily emerging as the new neutral as we inch closer to the new year, and lucky for our winter design schemes, the hue really is as versatile as it seems. Paired with powdery blues, bold crimsons, and even minty greens, chocolate brown grounds nearly any palette and matches every metallic hue.

    “I’m particularly drawn to chocolate brown as an unexpected foundation for holiday color palettes. It's incredibly rich and versatile. I love the idea of moving beyond traditional red and green and allowing the existing colors of a room to inform the holiday decor. You can create something incredibly festive through tonal layering, subtle metallic accents, and variations in material,” Flanigan explains.

    Survey Finds 84% of Organizations Reported at Least One AI-Related Incident in the Past Year

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Companies are running into problems as they give artificial intelligence more control over critical business applications, with 84% reporting at least one AI-related incident in the past year, according to a upcoming survey from identity security firm Delinea.
    • The manufacturer's 2026 Application Access Governance report found that some organizations have experienced incorrect financial transactions and AI actions they couldn't trace or explain.
    • The findings are based on an independent survey of 1,000 senior finance and finance technology leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Companies are running into problems as they give artificial intelligence more control over critical business applications, with 84% reporting at least one AI-related incident in the past year, according to a upcoming survey from identity security firm Delinea.

    The manufacturer's 2026 Application Access Governance report found that some organizations have experienced incorrect financial transactions and AI actions they couldn't trace or explain. The findings raise concerns about whether enterprises have enough oversight of AI systems that can make decisions and take actions on their own.

    The findings are based on an independent survey of 1,000 senior finance and finance technology leaders in the United States and United Kingdom. The AI-specific analysis included 879 respondents whose organizations use the technology in critical business applications.

    The report found that 35% of surveyed organizations have deployed AI agents capable of taking actions within business applications. However, only 11% of organizations using AI said their governance and security controls were keeping pace with deployment.

    Delinea also found gaps in centralized visibility into agent deployment and permissions, including who owns agents and who approved their use.

    Some respondents reported segregation-of-duties conflicts involving AI, while others identified agents that continued operating after the employees who deployed them had left the organization.

    Sources indicate that the research also highlighted gaps in monitoring access across business systems. Only 46% of respondents said they continuously monitor and manage cumulative access risks across applications.

    Those gaps can make it difficult to identify segregation-of-duties conflicts, in which a person or agent has permissions across systems that should be kept separate.

    Despite those issues, 95% of respondents mentioned they were confident their access controls would withstand scrutiny in an external audit.

    However, 26% reported access-related audit findings that had recurred in consecutive years, while 25% noted some findings had remained unresolved for three or more years.

    Only 22% of organizations had a single named owner for each application, with ownership tracked in one system of record.

    Meanwhile, 60% reported an increase over the past two years in the number of critical applications operating outside the scope of access governance or Sarbanes-Oxley Act compliance.

    The findings highlight the oversight challenges associated with giving AI agents authority to act within business systems, particularly when organizations cannot consistently identify who owns an agent or trace its actions.

    Frank Vukovits, chief security scientist at Delinea, remarked organizations remain responsible for the actions AI agents take within their systems.

    Recent findings suggest that "When an agent can approve a transaction or change permissions, the business owns the outcome. You need to know what every agent can do, who owns it, and who approved it, before an auditor asks or your financials are misstated," Vukovits noted.

    For the full report, go to the Delinea site.

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

    According to recent reports, in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines fresh guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (602 w)

    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Report: Cyber Criminals Move Toward More Targeted Phishing Attacks

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cyber criminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, increasingly using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a new report from KnowBe4.
    • The tech giant's Phishing Threat Trends Report, Vol.
    • Rather than sending the same fraudulent message to thousands of people, criminals are spending more time researching their targets and creating convincing messages that appear to come from trusted coworkers, businesses, and technology platforms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cyber criminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, increasingly using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a new report from KnowBe4. The security firm found that spear-phishing attacks increased 41% over the past year.

    The tech giant's Phishing Threat Trends Report, Vol. 8 found that overall phishing volume increased 29.8% year over year. Organizations received an average of one dangerous e-mail for every 733 messages, but the bigger concern is how attackers are changing their approach.

    Rather than sending the same fraudulent message to thousands of people, criminals are spending more time researching their targets and creating convincing messages that appear to come from trusted coworkers, businesses, and technology platforms.

    The findings are based on threat data from KnowBe4 Defend, the manufacturer's inbound e-mail security platform, which processes approximately 1.15 billion event signals daily.

    KnowBe4 found that several traditional phishing methods declined significantly compared with 2025. Mobile-focused scams dropped 47.3%, advance-fee fraud fell 31.3%, and missed-message scams declined 11.3%.

    Meanwhile, spear phishing increased 41.1%, pre-attack reconnaissance rose 33.7%, and organization impersonation climbed 28%.

    The shift suggests that attackers are finding more value in carefully crafted scams that exploit existing business relationships and workplace routines.

    It has been revealed that business e-mail compromise (BEC) remains particularly common, accounting for 51.2% of phishing e-mails analyzed in the report. Human resources, finance departments, and executive leadership are among the most frequently targeted groups.

    Attackers also appear to be timing their campaigns around normal business activity. KnowBe4 found that 90.4% of phishing messages arrive Monday through Friday, with Monday accounting for the largest share at 20.6%.

    One of the report's more troubling findings involves the growing use of legitimate technology platforms to deliver malicious content.

    KnowBe4 found that phishing attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the previous quarter.

    According to recent reports, that includes AI services, where attackers are taking advantage of trusted domains to host fake developer consoles, login prompts, and credential-stealing pages. The report also identified a 228% increase in AI-brand impersonation attacks between March and August.

    Because these malicious pages can operate on legitimate domains with valid security certificates, customers may not see the usual warning signs associated with suspicious websites.

    "For years, security advice has focused on a predictable checklist: Check the sender address, hover over the link, and look for the padlock," said Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence at KnowBe4.

    "While still foundational, that guidance is becoming less useful by the day.".

    The findings echo a recent report about management software and AI e-mail assistants. Research from Fortra and Barracuda highlighted how criminals are using legitimate administrative tools and hidden AI instructions to manipulate users and compromise systems.

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

    Sources indicate that in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines newly introduced guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint.

    #89227. Study: Sign-In Problems Are Primary Drivers of Help Desk Tickets

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (416 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Study: Sign-In Problems Are Primary Drivers of Help Desk Tickets

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network complications can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a fresh study from ControlUp.
    • Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations manufacturer identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) issues as major drivers of support demand.
    • In a recent development, at one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network complications can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a fresh study from ControlUp.

    Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations manufacturer identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) issues as major drivers of support demand.

    In a recent development, at one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems. Meanwhile, 87% of network and phone tickets were reassigned between teams, compared with 20% of account tickets.

    MFA enrollment and re-enrollment problems appeared at 40% of organizations, with one in five linking these problems to employees replacing or upgrading their phones. Virtual desktop problems appeared at 55% of organizations analyzed.

    Traditional phone support remained a major channel for IT assistance.

    According to recent reports, among organizations that recorded how support requests were submitted, 57% reported that phone calls accounted for approximately two-thirds or more of contacts. At one organization, that figure reached 99%.

    Machine-generated tickets from monitoring, security, backup, and patching systems appeared at half of the organizations studied. At 15%, automated tickets represented between 25% and 50% of all requests.

    The research covered enterprises across retail, healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, construction, energy, and IT services.

    ControlUp remarked the findings highlight the need to evaluate recurring problems and their operational impact rather than relying solely on ticket volume and resolution speed.

    "IT organizations have traditionally measured support performance by how quickly they close tickets, but that doesn't tell the whole story," said Simon Townsend, senior vice president of marketing and office of the CTO at ControlUp.

    "A password reset that takes a few minutes and an infrastructure failure that disrupts an entire location shouldn't carry the same operational weight.".

    For more information, go to the ControlUp site.

    California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a fresh model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

    OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the company says has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

    Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity manufacturer NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

    #89221. The Watches of Grand Theft Auto 6 (and Their Real-Life Inspiration)

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (499 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    The Watches of Grand Theft Auto 6 (and Their Real-Life Inspiration)

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (499 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For one glorious moment, the world appears to be united.
    • And amid all the fast cars, guns, nightclubs, and criminal capers, there's something else we pay attention to here at Esquire HQ: the watches!
    • Industry observers note that rockstar Games' latest blockbuster reportedly features 34 "collectible" luxury watches scattered throughout its fictional version of Florida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For one glorious moment, the world appears to be united. Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived, to near-universal acclaim, with millions of people abandoning work, school, and presumably all their other responsibilities to explore the streets of Vice City. In these divided times, it's enough to warm the cockles of your heart.

    And amid all the fast cars, guns, nightclubs, and criminal capers, there's something else we pay attention to here at Esquire HQ: the watches!

    Industry observers note that rockstar Games' latest blockbuster reportedly features 34 "collectible" luxury watches scattered throughout its fictional version of Florida. But that's only part of the story. GTA VI also has its own watch brands, although some of the designs look ... suspiciously familiar.

    There's Crowex (a dead ringer for Rolex), Takio (distinctly Casio-adjacent), and Covgari, whose watches owe more to Audemars Piguet than the Italian-o jeweller its name suggests.

    From gold Day-Dates to pocket-money Casio digitals, here are some of our favorite real-world watches that appear to have inspired the game's timepieces.

    According to recent reports, the gold Crowex is a near dead ringer for the Rolex Day-Date 40 (ref. 228238). The fluted bezel, black dial, and day window at 12 o'clock are all present and correct, although the bracelet differs somewhat from Rolex's iconic President. The Day-Date celebrates its 70th anniversary this year. Evidently, it remains the universal symbol of having made it, even in the virtual world.

    It has been revealed that the silver chronograph worn by a character overlooking Vice City has more than a passing resemblance to the mighty Daytona. The round case, contrasting sub-dials, and metal bracelet suggest that famous racing chronograph. As we know, the Daytona is one of the world's most sought-after sports watches, making it a natural fit for GTA's world of expensive cars, conspicuous consumption, and bling.

    Sources indicate that brian Heder, a veteran drug smuggler, wears a metal sports watch that certainly seems to recall Rolex's Sub. There's the substantial case, dark dial, and the bracelet. The Submariner has been a fixture of luxury watchmaking since 1953, and its more ostentatious steel-and-gold versions would be right at home on the streets of Vice City.

    In-game equivalent: Takio Digital Watch.

    Jason Duval, one of GTA VI's two protagonists, wears a chunky digital watch resembling something from Casio's Pro Trek range. The large circular display, prominent buttons and rugged case certainly suggest its something from the range of the Japanese juggernaut. A more practical choice than the gold watches favored by some of his associates.

    In-game equivalent: Takio Digital Watch.

    Not everyone in Vice City is wearing a gold Rollie lookalike. The Takio F-BLAST is an unmistakable nod to Casio's inexpensive digital classics, particularly the bestselling F-91W. It has the familiar rectangular display, black dial surround, and simple, functional design. There's even a more colorful version, with a red case and two-tone metal bracelet, spotted in the game's Hamlet Thrift store.

    As spotted by watch Instagram account @geesgshock.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a upcoming Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.
    • The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025.
    • A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a upcoming Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

    The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

    A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

    Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

    According to recent reports, the report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

    The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

    "Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

    Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

    An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

    According to recent reports, menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

    It has been revealed that the report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

    According to recent reports, A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG notes ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

    That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

    According to recent reports, for enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

    Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

    #89211. Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (468 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.
    • According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.
    • The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

    The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

    The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

    Industry observers note that docuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

    The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

    In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

    Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

    The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

    Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

    Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

    Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

    CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

    Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing customers to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

    Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

    The manufacturer also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.
